task: strike a deal on a peer-to-peer marketplace (Facebook Marketplace, eBay, Craigslist): browse listings, assess the item and the counterparty's trustworthiness, message or bid/make an offer, agree on price and handoff, and commit — platform checkout or an agreed pickup in the message thread; complete when a purchase confirmation, accepted offer, or agreed deal in messages is on screen. Selling — listing an item and closing with a buyer — is the same ask from the other side and belongs. Surface pinned: a marketplace website or app. Variants: booking a service visit (seeded variant), retail shopping on Amazon-style stores, and apartment hunting do not belong.

tree.label: Strike a deal on a marketplace
tree.note: do 1. buyers then run 2, 3 and one of 4, 5 or 6 - repeat 2.7 and 3 until a listing passes the check (ruQX inspects three, DrZ5 leaves one for another). 4 on Facebook Marketplace; 5 on an eBay auction; 6 on an eBay fixed-price listing - DrZ5 runs 5 up to the payment wall and then 6 on a different listing. sellers run 7 where the item is in the room (dYz5, WwXj), then 8, then 9. tPLF runs 8 and 9 and then 4 on the same account. no keeper reaches a payment or a reply.

children.label: Get onto the marketplace
children.note: 1.1 in every keeper. 1.2 only where the platform asks, and both keepers who hit it are cut past the form. 1.3 where the session starts signed in. 1.4 for eBay sellers, whose form lives in the Seller Hub. 1.5 is one keeper's tour and comes before anything else.

questions.question: Is the listing on screen the one you asked for, or a leftover from before?
questions.why: The screen displays a specific Bosch rotary hammer listing, but clicking the eBay logo resets the view to the homepage to start a fresh search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to find their actual desired item if the agent mistakenly proceeds with purchasing the currently displayed product.
questions.check: Does the page show an item listing rather than the homepage search box, and does the item name match the requested item?
questions.say_example: The page opened on an old <Bosch rotary hammer> listing. That isn't what you asked for. I'm starting a fresh search.

questions.question: Should you log in with your existing account or create a new one?
questions.why: The login screen presents fields for existing credentials alongside a 'Create new account' button, forcing a choice that will impact your marketplace reputation.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might create a new, untrusted profile instead of leveraging your established account's reputation to secure better deals.
questions.check: Does the page show a sign-in form with email and password fields, and a 'Create new account' option?
questions.say_example: The site wants you signed in. I don't type passwords. Sign in, then tell me to continue.

questions.question: Is the name in the greeting at the top yours?
questions.why: Confirming the 'Hi testing!' greeting ensures your account is active before you use the search bar to find items.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the immediate reassurance of seeing their own name confirming a successful account setup before diving into the marketplace.
questions.check: What name does the greeting at the top of the page show, and does it match the account name given?
questions.say_example: The site says hi to <testing>. That's not you. I'm signing out before we go on.

questions.question: Is the site blocking you from making a new listing?
questions.why: A prominent red banner explicitly states that you are unable to create new listings until your Payoneer account is verified.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user wastes time because the agent attempts a listing process that is guaranteed to fail due to the unresolved account restriction.
questions.check: Does a banner say new listings are blocked, and what does it say has to happen first?
questions.say_example: The site says you can't list anything until <your Payoneer account is verified>. I can't do that part. Sort it out, then tell me to continue.

children.label: Find a listing
children.note: 2.1 first on Facebook - the app keepers set the radius before typing anything. one of 2.2 to 2.4 raises candidates. 2.5 and 2.6 narrow where the strategy needs it - half the keepers open the filters and apply none. then 2.7; a rejected listing comes back here from 3.

questions.question: Are the search location and radius the ones you want?
questions.why: The screen shows a location label set to 'Derby - 10 km', which determines if the items shown are within a practical distance for you to pick up.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally decide exactly how far you are willing to travel for the right deal.
questions.check: What location and radius does the search label show, and do they match the location asked for?
questions.say_example: The search is set to <Derby>, <10 km>. You're in <Nottingham>. Changing it.

questions.question: Are all the results inside your radius, or are some from further away?
questions.why: Marketplaces frequently ignore strict distance filters when local inventory is low, silently inserting listings from outside your requested area.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might initiate a purchase for an item that requires an impossibly long drive for local pickup because it trusted the filter to be absolute.
questions.check: Do any results show a distance greater than the set radius, or a label saying they come from further away?
questions.say_example: Some of these are outside your <10 km>. The <sofa> is <40 km> away. I'm skipping those.

questions.question: Should you take one of the site's search suggestions, or keep your own wording?
questions.why: The dropdown showed specific categories like 'cd player' and 'cd lot', which narrow the results, whereas the broad term casts a wider net for items to bid on.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might automatically select a specific suggestion, depriving you of the chance to browse a broad category for unexpected deals.
questions.check: Which search suggestions does the dropdown show under the typed term?
questions.say_example: Searched for <cd> - kept your wording over the suggested <cd player>

questions.question: Which subcategory should you open?
questions.why: The screen displays diverse industrial subcategories like Heavy Equipment and Light Equipment & Tools, so selecting the right one narrows the listings to the specific items you need.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might select the wrong equipment category, wasting time browsing irrelevant listings instead of the specific tools you actually want.
questions.check: Which subcategories does the page list?
questions.say_example: Opened <Light Equipment & Tools>

questions.question: Which of your recently viewed items do you want to revisit?
questions.why: The homepage displays a history of items you've looked at, such as shoes, phones, and a Nintendo Switch, requiring you to select which one to pursue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might guess incorrectly about which previously viewed item you are actually ready to buy.
questions.check: Which items does the recently viewed row show?
questions.say_example: Reopened the <Nintendo Switch> from your recently viewed

questions.question: Do you want only auctions in the results?
questions.why: The screen displays filter tabs like 'Auction' and 'Buy It Now', which determine whether you can bid on the item or must purchase it outright.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose your preferred buying format, which dictates whether you can hunt for a bargain through bidding or secure the item immediately.
questions.check: Which listing-format tabs does the page show, and which one is selected?
questions.say_example: Filtered to auctions only, since you asked to bid

questions.question: Do you want only items listed in the last day?
questions.why: The screen provides a 'Date listed' filter that lets you narrow the search to the freshest inventory.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to prioritize newly listed items or browse a wider, older selection.
questions.check: What does the 'Date listed' filter show as selected?
questions.say_example: Filtered to listings from the last day

questions.question: What maximum price should you set to stay within your budget?
questions.why: Entering a limit in the maximum price filter ensures the search results only display items you can actually afford.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to define their exact financial constraints and decide how strictly to enforce their budget.
questions.check: What value is in the maximum price field?
questions.say_example: Set the max price to <100>

questions.question: Which filters do you want on the results?
questions.why: The filter dialog offers options like condition, price, and local pickup, which determine the relevance of the listings you will see.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify your exact preferences for item condition, price range, and delivery method.
questions.check: How many results does the page report, and which filters are applied?
questions.say_example: Found <2,400>. You asked for <local pickup>, so I'm filtering to that. That leaves <38>.

questions.question: Should you change the default sort order to find auctions ending soon?
questions.why: The default 'Best Match' sort shows over 10 million results with sponsored 'Buy It Now' items at the top, which hides live auctions that are about to close.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your preferred bidding strategy, such as targeting auctions that are ending soonest to snipe a good deal.
questions.check: Which sort order is selected, and are the top results marked Sponsored?
questions.say_example: The default sort puts sponsored Buy It Now items first. I'm sorting by ending soonest instead.

questions.question: Which listing should you open?
questions.why: The grid displays diverse options like a phone, laptops, and a motorcycle, and your selection determines the specific product and price point you will pursue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent choose means you lose the ability to pick an item that genuinely interests you or fits your specific budget.
questions.check: Which listings are shown, with title, price, condition, location and end time for each?
questions.say_example: Two that fit. The <LG 55 inch>, <150>, <used>, <5 km> away. The <Samsung 50 inch>, <120>, but the seller is new. Which one? Say <LG> or <Samsung>.

questions.question: Do you still want this sponsored listing with its high delivery fee?
questions.why: The first result is a sponsored listing with a $27.55 delivery fee that nearly doubles the $28.99 item price.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user ends up overpaying because the agent blindly clicked the first sponsored result without evaluating the exorbitant shipping cost.
questions.check: Is the first result marked Sponsored, and what delivery fee does it show against the item price?
questions.say_example: The first result is sponsored. Delivery is <27.55> on a <28.99> item. I'm skipping it.

questions.question: Did the auction already close while you were browsing the search results?
questions.why: The search results page can become stale, displaying items that have just ended (e.g., 'Ended'), meaning any attempt to bid on them will fail.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent wastes time clicking into and attempting to bid on closed auctions instead of refreshing the page to find active listings.
questions.check: Does the listing show 'Ended' or a countdown at zero?
questions.say_example: That one ended while we were looking. Skipping it.

children.label: Vet the listing and seller
children.note: 3.1 in every keeper. 3.2 and 3.3 where the buyer bothers - three keepers skip the description on purpose. 3.4 on every Facebook listing and on most eBay ones. 3.5 only on Facebook, where the handoff is a drive. 3.6 is a check nobody runs, and every eBay keeper needed it. 3.7 is one keeper, after the checkout attempt. a rejected listing sends the buyer back to 2.7.

questions.question: Is this item actually free, or is the price misleading?
questions.why: The listing shows a price of Rs0 for a new item at a business location, which often indicates a deceptive placeholder price rather than a genuinely free item.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the intuition to spot bait-and-switch business listings that use fake zero-dollar prices to lure in buyers.
questions.check: Does the price show as 0 or Free, and is the listing from a business or marked new?
questions.say_example: It says <Rs0>, but it's a shop listing for a new item. That zero is a placeholder. The real price isn't on the page.

questions.question: Does the listing carry the 'Authenticity Guarantee' badge?
questions.why: For high-value items like sneakers or watches, this visual badge is the only guarantee that the platform will physically inspect the item before forwarding it to you, mitigating the risk of fakes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the critical risk-mitigation of platform verification, potentially spending hundreds on a counterfeit because the agent couldn't 'see' the badge.
questions.check: Does the listing show an 'Authenticity Guarantee' label?
questions.say_example: This one has the site's authenticity check. They inspect it before it ships to you.

questions.question: Is the price in another currency, like C $ or AU $, instead of yours?
questions.why: A tiny prefix before the dollar sign drastically changes the actual cost due to exchange rates and bank conversion fees, which is easy to miss if you aren't looking closely at the screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user ends up paying unexpected foreign transaction fees and a different base price because the agent only parsed the numeric value and the dollar sign.
questions.check: What currency prefix appears before the price, and does it differ from the account's currency?
questions.say_example: The price is <C $250>. That's in <Canadian dollars>. Your bank may add a fee on top.

questions.question: Are you OK with the condition and description the listing gives?
questions.why: Reviewing the item specifics ensures you know exactly what you are buying, such as the fact that the SNES bundle is used but tested.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally judge if the specific used condition and included items meet their personal standards.
questions.check: What condition does the listing state, and what does the condition note say?
questions.say_example: Listed as <used>, <tested and working>

questions.question: Does the description mention flaws or missing parts that the title and condition line leave out?
questions.why: The screen provides both image thumbnails and an item description section, and relying solely on photos might cause you to miss important flaws or missing parts noted in the text.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally weigh the visual evidence against the seller's written disclosures to determine if the item meets their standards.
questions.check: Does the description mention flaws or missing parts that the title and condition line leave out?
questions.say_example: The description says <no charger included>. The title doesn't mention that.

questions.question: Do the close-up photos show damage the description leaves out?
questions.why: Inspecting the enlarged gallery images of the console's screen and back helps verify the seller's claims about its condition before you commit to buying.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally judge the physical wear and tear visible in the photos to decide if the item meets your own standards.
questions.check: Do photo captions, alt text, or text visible in the photos mention damage that the condition line doesn't?
questions.say_example: The close-up photo shows <a crack on the screen>. The listing says <good condition>.

questions.question: Do the specs in the images match the model listed in the title?
questions.why: The listing title claimed the TV was a 65-inch Q60A, but the second image clearly showed specs for a 55-inch Q70C model.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user risks purchasing a different, smaller TV than advertised or falling for a deceptive listing.
questions.check: Does the model or size printed in any photo match the model and size in the title?
questions.say_example: The title says <65 inch Q60A>. The label in the second photo says <55 inch Q70C>. That's a different TV.

questions.question: Is there text like 'Cash only', 'Firm', or a phone number written on the photos?
questions.why: Sellers frequently overlay text on images to bypass platform rules or text filters, establishing strict payment or contact rules outside the machine-readable description.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might commit to a transaction assuming standard platform payment is accepted, only to find out at handoff that the seller demands physical cash.
questions.check: Is there text written into the photos, such as 'Cash only', 'Firm', or a phone number?
questions.say_example: The photo has <Cash only, firm> written on it. That's not in the description. The seller won't take offers.

questions.question: Do the seller's recent feedback comments say anything the positive percentage hides?
questions.why: Reading the actual text of the reviews, such as 'Fast ship' and 'As described,' verifies that the 100% positive rating comes from genuine, satisfactory transactions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your own intuition to determine if the written reviews feel authentic and trustworthy.
questions.check: What do the seller's most recent feedback comments say?
questions.say_example: The seller is <98%> positive, but the last three comments say <item not as described>.

questions.question: What feedback percentage and rating count does the seller show?
questions.why: The screen displays the seller's 98.9% positive rating, which is crucial for determining if they are a trustworthy counterparty.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally evaluate the seller's reputation and decide your own comfort level with the transaction risk.
questions.check: What feedback percentage and rating count does the seller show?
questions.say_example: Seller is <98.9%> positive from <1,200> ratings.

questions.question: Is the seller named on the listing the same one the search results showed?
questions.why: The screen shows the seller listed as 'wnymaets' in the search results but 'Party Zealot' on the product details page, which is a major red flag for a scam.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to spot suspicious inconsistencies that suggest a fraudulent listing or untrustworthy counterparty.
questions.check: Does the seller name on the listing match the seller name shown in the search results?
questions.say_example: The results said the seller was <wnymaets>. The listing says <Party Zealot>. That's two names for one listing. I'd skip it.

questions.question: Is this a new seller account?
questions.why: The seller profile shows they joined Facebook recently, which is a common red flag for scam accounts created solely to post fraudulent listings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to apply their street smarts to avoid scammers who spin up new accounts to defraud buyers.
questions.check: What join date does the seller profile show?
questions.say_example: This seller joined <last month>, so the account is new. Be careful with this one.

questions.question: What pickup location and distance does the listing show?
questions.why: The screen shows a bottom sheet with options to open the item's location in a map application to evaluate the travel time.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might skip checking the exact driving distance, committing you to a pickup location that is inconveniently far away.
questions.check: What pickup location and distance does the listing show?
questions.say_example: Pickup is in <Derby>, <12 km> away

questions.question: Is the item pickup only, and how big does the listing say it is?
questions.why: The listing is for a 65-inch TV for local pickup, which will not fit in a standard car and requires a large SUV or van to transport safely.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might commit to a local pickup deal for an item they physically cannot transport, leading to a canceled transaction or unexpected rental costs.
questions.check: Is the item pickup only, and what size does the listing state?
questions.say_example: Pickup only, and it's a <65 inch TV>. That won't fit in most cars.

questions.question: Does the area the map labels match the town named in the listing?
questions.why: The text might just say a city name, but the visual map circle reveals if the seller is actually located in a neighborhood that requires a toll or heavy traffic routing to reach.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user commits to a local pickup that is technically within their distance radius but practically a nightmare or expensive to drive to.
questions.check: Does the area the map labels match the town named in the listing?
questions.say_example: The listing says <Oakland>. The map puts it in <Alameda>, <across the bridge>.

questions.question: Does the listing page show the delivery fee the search results showed?
questions.why: The search results displayed a $6.99 delivery fee that was absent on the item detail page, obscuring the true total cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses financial predictability and might end up paying more than expected if hidden shipping fees are applied at checkout.
questions.check: Does the listing's pricing block show the same delivery fee the search result showed?
questions.say_example: The results showed <6.99> delivery. The listing page doesn't show it. The real total is closer to <35.98>.

questions.question: What does shipping add to the item price?
questions.why: The listing shows a $12.25 shipping fee, meaning your $75.00 maximum bid actually commits you to a potential total of $87.25.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to strictly control their total out-of-pocket expenses if the agent fails to account for added shipping fees.
questions.check: What item price and shipping fee does the listing show, and what do they total?
questions.say_example: It's <75>, plus <12.25> shipping. So <87.25> total.

questions.question: What buyer protection covers this listing?
questions.why: Checking the 'eBay Money Back Guarantee' and return details ensures you know your options if the item doesn't arrive or match the description.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally assess the platform's buyer protection policies and decide if the return conditions are acceptable for your risk tolerance.
questions.check: Does the listing show a money-back guarantee, and what return terms?
questions.say_example: Covered by the site's money-back guarantee, returns for <30 days>

questions.question: Who does the return policy say pays for return shipping?
questions.why: The return policy explicitly states that while returns are accepted for 30 days, the buyer is responsible for the return shipping cost, which reduces the final refund amount.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might assume a '30-day return' means a full refund, losing the awareness that they will bear the financial cost of shipping it back.
questions.check: Who does the return policy say pays for return shipping, and what does return shipping cost?
questions.say_example: Returns are accepted for <30 days>, but you'd pay the return shipping. On this one that's about <130>, most of the refund.

children.label: Message or make an offer
children.note: the Facebook commit, and eBay's Contact seller. 4.1 or 4.2 on the listing, then 4.3 where the platform confirms it. 4.4 where the sheet is offered; ruQX stages one and drops it. 4.5 is never on camera - every keeper stops at Send.

questions.question: Should you send the seller the pre-filled message asking if it's still available?
questions.why: The screen shows a ready-to-send message prompt asking about availability, presenting the choice to either initiate contact or return to the search results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether this specific listing is worth pursuing or if you should back out to keep browsing other options.
questions.check: What message text is in the box, and who is it addressed to?
questions.say_example: Ready to message <seller> about the <TV>. It says <Is this still available?>. It's in <Derby>, <12 km> away. Send it, or change the wording?

questions.question: Does the message about to go out share a phone number, email, or payment app the site warns against?
questions.why: The messaging window displays a strict warning against exchanging contact information or transacting outside the platform to prevent fraud.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose direct control over ensuring your messages strictly comply with the platform's safety warnings against sharing personal contact information.
questions.check: Does the message text contain a phone number, email address, or payment app name, and does the page show a warning against sharing those?
questions.say_example: The site warns not to share contact details here. I've taken <the phone number> out of the message.

questions.question: Does the thread show the seller as active now, or your message as seen?
questions.why: These subtle visual indicators tell you if the counterparty is currently online and looking at your message, dictating whether you should wait for an immediate reply or move on.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the situational awareness to negotiate in real-time, as the agent might fire off a message and close the session right as the seller starts typing.
questions.check: Does the thread show 'Active now' or 'Seen' next to the seller?
questions.say_example: The seller has seen your message. No reply yet.

questions.question: Does the chat thread show the message as sent?
questions.why: The video cuts away to the marketplace grid without showing a standard sent confirmation in the chat thread, relying only on a teal checkmark next to the send button.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses absolute certainty that their communication was successfully delivered to the seller, risking a missed connection on the item.
questions.check: Does the thread show the message with a sent or delivered mark?
questions.say_example: The message didn't go through. It's still in the box. Trying again.

questions.question: What amount should you offer for this item?
questions.why: The screen presents preset offer amounts and a custom option, requiring a decision on how much to bid before sending the offer.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over their negotiation strategy, including the exact amount to offer or the choice to back out before committing.
questions.check: What offer amounts does the page present, and what is the asking price?
questions.say_example: Asking is <200>. The site suggests <180>, <170>, or <160>. How much do you want to offer?

questions.question: Did the site turn your offer down automatically?
questions.why: Sellers can configure hidden auto-decline thresholds, meaning your offer might be instantly rejected by the system rather than sent to the seller for review.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user misses the opportunity to negotiate further because the agent assumes the proposal is pending and waits for a human response.
questions.check: Does the page say the offer was declined automatically or immediately after sending?
questions.say_example: Your <150> offer was declined automatically. It never reached the seller.

questions.question: Has the seller come back with a counter-offer?
questions.why: In negotiations, sellers often reject the initial offer and propose a higher price, which you must manually accept, decline, or counter again before the deal expires.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might let a time-sensitive counter-offer expire, losing the item, or automatically accept a price higher than your actual limit.
questions.check: Does the thread show a counter-offer from the seller, and what amount?
questions.say_example: The seller came back with <180>. That's <20> over your offer. Accept, counter, or walk away?

questions.question: Did the seller ask to talk or pay by text, Zelle, or CashApp instead?
questions.why: Scammers frequently try to bypass platform protections by requesting direct wire transfers or phone numbers in the messaging thread.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses their financial protection and could be scammed if the agent blindly complies with an off-platform payment request.
questions.check: Does the seller's message ask to pay or talk by text, Zelle, CashApp, or otherwise outside the site?
questions.say_example: The seller wants to be paid by <Zelle>. Outside the site you have no protection. I'm staying in the site's messages.

questions.question: Has the seller seen your message and not replied for over a day?
questions.why: On peer-to-peer marketplaces, sellers frequently ghost buyers; recognizing this allows you to stop waiting and move on to a different listing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might indefinitely wait for a dead lead instead of pivoting to purchase a backup item.
questions.check: Does the thread show 'Seen' with a timestamp more than 24 hours old and no reply after it?
questions.say_example: The seller read your message <yesterday> and hasn't answered. I'll move to the next listing unless you say wait.

questions.question: Did the seller mention a flaw or missing part in chat that the listing left out?
questions.why: Sellers sometimes wait until a buyer is actively negotiating or emotionally invested to reveal that an item is broken, locked, or missing its charger.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user ends up overpaying for a damaged item because the agent failed to re-evaluate the deal based on new negative information revealed privately in the DMs.
questions.check: Does a seller message mention a defect or missing part that the listing does not?
questions.say_example: The seller just said <the charger is missing>. The listing didn't mention that.

questions.question: Did the seller's last message change the pickup place or time you agreed?
questions.why: Sellers often bait-and-switch the meetup spot to somewhere less convenient or less safe right before the handoff.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user might be committed to traveling to an unsafe or distant location because the agent agreed to a last-minute logistics change.
questions.check: Does the seller's latest message name a different place or time from the one agreed earlier in the thread?
questions.say_example: The seller moved the meetup from <the mall> to <their apartment>. That's a change from what you agreed.

questions.question: How much will you bid, or will you use the Buy It Now option?
questions.why: With only 45 seconds left and zero bids, you must decide whether to risk a minimum $2.00 bid or secure the item immediately for $4.50.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over their personal bidding strategy and risk tolerance for securing the item.
questions.check: What current bid, minimum bid, time left, and Buy It Now price does the listing show?
questions.say_example: Current bid is <2>, with <45 seconds> left. Or buy it now for <4.50>. What's your maximum? Or say buy now.

questions.question: Should you add this item to your watchlist instead of placing a bid right now?
questions.why: The auction has only 18 minutes left at $51.00, so adding it to a watchlist allows you to monitor the final bidding activity before committing your money.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the strategic choice of whether to monitor the auction's final minutes or place an immediate bid.
questions.check: Does the page have a watchlist button, and how long is left?
questions.say_example: Added to your watchlist - ends in <18 minutes>

questions.question: When should you come back to bid at the end?
questions.why: The screen displays the exact auction end time, which dictates when you need to be present to place a strategic last-minute bid without driving up the price early.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the strategic control of deciding exactly when to intervene and the personal thrill of executing a last-second bid yourself.
questions.check: What auction end time does the page show?
questions.say_example: This auction ends <Thursday at 7:42 pm>. You'll know if you won then.

questions.question: Does clicking 'Place bid' only open the bid form, or does it commit a bid straight away?
questions.why: The screen shows an eBay item page with a blue 'Place bid' button that must be clicked to open the bidding interface.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over determining the exact maximum bid amount and the strategic timing of placing the bid.
questions.check: Does pressing 'Place bid' open a form with an amount box, or does it place the bid straight away?
questions.say_example: Opened the bid form - the button only opens it, nothing is bid yet

children.label: Clear the payment gate
children.note: 5.4.1 as the prompts appear, then 5.4.2 for an account with nothing on file - both keepers who hit it back out. 5.4.3 is the pass-through case: the card is read inside the modal and no wall appears.
